This page defines shared page-level frontmatter conventions for the knowledge garden.
Page-level attributes are bare key:: value lines at the top of the file, before any bullet. --- fences around them are illegal in Logseq; if they appear, unwrap them.
alias:: for more convenient or alternate names
In Logseq, if page [[Super Long Name]] has frontmatter alias:: [[Shortname]], then clicking [[Shortname]] anywhere in the graph navigates to [[Super Long Name]].

On a work, recording or other creation, lists the Logseq/Entity/Identity pages credited as its creators or artists, in published order.
Comma-separated identity-page links. A joint release can carry created-by-identities:: [[Bibio]], [[Dorian Concept]].
A name that is only a person's ordinary biographical name can use created-by:: or performer:: directly without a separate identity page.
created-by:: records known people who made the particular work or recording; performer:: records known performers. Neither property is inferred from identity membership alone.
An identity credit can be known even when individual contributors are unknown. In that case the identity credit stands on its own.

The first credited identity supplies the namespace when the creation's entity definition uses identity-based placement. Logseq/Entity/Music/Recording and Logseq/Entity/Music/Work define musical placement.

logseq-created-time-year:: - links an entity to its creation year, decade, or century
The value is a link to the matching Logseq/Entity/Time/Year instance, at whatever precision is actually known — a specific year, or its decade or century when only that much is known.

Distinct from date-created::: that property holds the display-quality date value (day, month, or year, per Logseq/Date) and does not always resolve to a Logseq/Entity/Time/Year page. logseq-created-time-year:: always does, so every entity created in a given year, decade, or century collects there as a backlink regardless of the entity's own type.
Applies broadly, to any entity whose creation year is known: books, movies, podcast episodes, essays, musical compositions, works of art, and others.
Set alongside date-created::, not instead of it, when both are known.
logseq-entity:: marks a page as an instance of a Logseq entity
The value should be the relevant entity definition page, such as Logseq/Entity/Game, Logseq/Entity/Software/Project, or Logseq/Entity/Question.
logseq-entity:: marks a page as an instance of a Logseq entity
A page that models more than one entity lists each marker, comma-separated, primary entity first. Logseq/Entity describes multiple entity membership.

The purpose of see-also:: is to aid discovery of distant, directly pages in the garden with a compelling discovery case, and which does not appear in the body of the page. It should be used very sparingly and rarely, including no more than 2-3 items, and it should almost never include pages that are immediate parent, child or siblings in the namespace hierarchy.

Logseq tags have a special impact on the Logseq UI, but their implementation is buggy and inconsistent. In addition, the human gardener's use of tags:: pre-dated the more mature Logseq/Entity entity system, and the human's rules for applying them are fuzzy and ill-defined. It's easier to use them incorrectly than to use them correctly.
As a result, their use is considered protected on existing pages: AI should not modify, add, or remove it unless explicit human instruction overrides the garden tagging rules.
For new pages, add tags:: only when the relevant page-type convention explicitly requires it or nearby pages establish the same pattern.

project name, lgskr for short at the CLI
Trilium — self-hosted hierarchical PKM with rich text; tagged in-garden as a PKM/Tool and cross-linked from Knowledge/Garden.

Hulunote — outliner-style notes as nested blocks, drag-and-drop reorder, bidirectional links and backlinks, daily notes, full-text search, Markdown import/export, MCP integration; Leptos + Rust UI web client with a Rust API backend and optional Tauri desktop packaging in the client repo.
IWE — plain-Markdown hierarchical knowledge graph with polyhierarchy and inclusion semantics, LSP support (VS Code, Neovim, Zed, Helix), CLI, and an MCP server for agent access; documentation hub.

Qipu — git-backed knowledge graph CLI in Rust (qipu-core crate) with typed links, value scoring, full-text search, and agent-oriented commands such as prime and context; oriented at durable research memory rather than interactive outliner editing.

Vulcan — Rust CLI for Obsidian-style vaults: graph-aware indexing, backlinks, tasks, interactive TUI, and safe vault mutations including link rewriting; page-centric vault model rather than Logseq block granularity.
Rucola — terminal Zettelkasten manager over Markdown with link graph navigation, filters, stats, and HTML export; complements editor-centric workflows without a block outliner UI.
mdzk — Rust toolkit that treats Zettelkasten Markdown as a compiled directed graph (static-site / publishing angle); under active iteration rather than a full Logseq-class interactive client.

Knowledge/Garden — definition of digital gardens / Zettelkasten, curated public examples, and a history thread that situates wikis, PKM, and the Roam/Obsidian-era graph-note wave alongside earlier tools.

Knowledge/Concept/Knowledge Base vs Knowledge Garden — contrasts organizational knowledge bases with personal gardening; useful for deciding what a rewrite must preserve versus what belongs to a different product shape.

How a day reads in this garden: 's own writing up top, the recurring sections, and the end-of-day change log. An agent writes the change log and nothing else here — the blocks above it are 's, neither written nor removed by an agent. The conventions live here in one place; subpages carry section-specific detail. Parallels Logseq/Entity.
Each day ends with a record of what changed in the graph, as two top-level blocks:
Each day ends with a record of what changed in the graph, as two top-level blocks:
Updated — pages that already existed and were edited today.
Each day ends with a record of what changed in the graph, as two top-level blocks:
and Updated are sibling top-level blocks — no parent wrapper and no intro line above them.

The line form is - # [[Filed]], with the bullet, which is the plurality across the graph and the only common form satisfying the bullet rule in .claude/rules/logseq-core.md. Where a journal's first line has lost its bullet, an editor save ate it rather than a person choosing.
A page appears under only one section per day. A page that was both created and edited today stays under only.
Lines are link-only: - [[Some/Page]]. No Created … / Updated … boilerplate and no inline action text; add at most one short child sentence when it genuinely helps a reader.
This is a curated snapshot of the day's adventures — a glimpse, not a full audit of every git change. Skip trivial stubs and noise.
When a section runs past a handful of links, cluster them under plain-text labels — bare words or short phrases (tuis, entities, git tasks), not [[wikilinks]].
Choose labels with the human; they should jog memory and name the day's real clusters of discovery, not generic bins.

Labels are alphabetized, under and under Updated alike. Items inside a label keep semantic order. The narrative above the change log is ordered however wrote it and is left alone. This holds for 2026-08-25 Tue onward; a journal already written stays as it is.

Above the change log, a day may carry topic-led blocks with editorial-style titles, and writes those. Logseq/Journal/Editorial headings describes how they are titled, for their use rather than an agent's. Three agent-written narrative blocks were deleted by hand from the 2026-08-18 Tue journal, and an agent following that page reproduced the deletion again on 2026-08-24 Mon.
Logseq/Journal/Section/Friction describes a section wrote once, on 2026-03-25 Wed, and no journal has carried since. Write it when they ask for it rather than expecting it in a day.
journals/2026_06_27.md — a topic-led narrative block up top, then and Updated as top-level blocks with grouped, link-only lists.

writes these headings. An agent writes the and Updated change log and nothing above it, so this page describes a human's titling practice rather than instructing an agent. An agent reading it as an instruction has twice put narrative blocks in a journal that were then deleted by hand.

Section titles should feel curated: wry, juxtaposed, a little magazine-like — in the spirit of Harper's, the Economist, the New Yorker. The outline should suggest tensions (tool vs platform, freedom vs friction) without explaining the joke in prose.
Cluster related bullets under one heading so the contrast between sections does the work, not just long flat lists.
Headings may use [[Topic]] links when the day is organized around entities or areas already tracked; wit is welcome but not mandatory every line.
"It's always Acronym-ious with AI" — wordplay on "acrimonious."
"The Art of the Side-Note" — elevating a minor detail.
"Tools That Think They're Platforms" — a wry observation.
Wordplay — play with the language ("Acronym-ious", "Freedom and/from").
Contrast — surface a tension (old/new, free/constrained, tool/platform).
